title: Hypothesis Formulation - Canadian SR&ED Tax Credit Glossary
description: Explore why clear Hypothesis Formulation is a mandatory step in systematic R&D investigation in our Canadian SR&ED glossary.
summary: Hypothesis formulation is a required step in Canada's SR&ED tax incentive program: businesses claiming federal investment tax credits must show they formulated a specific hypothesis, an idea or proposed technological method consistent with known facts, to resolve a defined technological uncertainty, then tested it systematically and kept contemporaneous records, as the CRA and Canadian courts require.

body.text: Hypothesis formulation is a required step in Canada's SR&ED tax incentive program: businesses claiming federal investment tax credits must show they formulated a specific hypothesis, an idea or proposed technological method consistent with known facts, to resolve a defined technological uncertainty, then tested it systematically and kept contemporaneous records, as the CRA and Canadian courts require.

Between December 2024 and November 2026, Parliament enacted the most substantial expansion of the federal Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program in over a decade. On March 26, 2026, Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1) received Royal Assent, codifying—retroactively for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024—an increase in the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% SR&ED Investment Tax Credit (ITC) from $3.0 million to $6.0 million (superseding an interim $4.5 million proposal) and doubling the maximum annual refundable federal credit from $1.05 million to $2.10 million. Bill C-15 simultaneously widened the taxable capital phase-out range from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, extended the 35% enhanced credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) subject to a three-year average gross revenue phase-out (also available by election to Canadian-controlled private corporations), and restored eligibility for capital expenditures and equipment lease outlays incurred after December 15, 2024, subject to a 40% cash refundability cap on enhanced-rate capital credits. Administratively, the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) launched an optional Pre-Claim Approval process on April 1, 2026, while Federal Budget 2026 (tabled on November 5, 2026) proposed a $930 million commercialization expansion covering regulatory validation studies and intellectual property (IP) registration and maintenance expenses in lieu of a federal patent box. Provincially, Québec replaced eight legacy credits with the refundable Research, Innovation and Commercialization Tax Credit (CRIC) after March 25, 2025, British Columbia made its 10% credit permanent and aligned with the $6.0 million federal reforms, Saskatchewan raised its refundable CCPC threshold to $2.0 million, Ontario restored capital expenditure eligibility for its R&D credits while retaining its own expenditure caps, and Alberta maintained independent provincial caps and capital exclusions.
1. Executive Overview and the 2024–2026 Legislative Transformation
1.1 Fiscal Scale and Statutory Entitlement Mechanics

The Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program is the cornerstone of Canadian industrial innovation policy and the country's largest single source of non-dilutive R&D funding. Policy design and legislative amendments reside under the jurisdiction of the Department of Finance Canada, while day-to-day technical evaluation, financial verification, and tax credit disbursement are administered by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA). Unlike competitive grant programs that depend on discretionary selection committees or fixed annual budget envelopes, SR&ED operates as an open-ended statutory entitlement under the federal Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)): any taxpayer carrying on business in Canada whose R&D projects satisfy the statutory scientific and technological criteria and mandatory filing deadlines is legally entitled to claim the resulting tax deductions and investment tax credits.

Industry analyses citing CRA program disclosures confirm rapid growth in claim volume and fiscal value. During fiscal year 2024–2025, the CRA delivered $4.5 billion in SR&ED investment tax credits across more than 19,000 claimants and over 22,000 processed claims, with advisory tracking citing 22,758 claims and attributing 40.8% of allowed credits to software development alone. For the fiscal year ended March 31, 2026 (FY2025–2026), published analyses citing CRA reporting indicate $4.9 billion in ITCs claimed and $4.6 billion allowed across 23,677 processed claims, marking a roughly 50% climb in annual credit disbursements since fiscal 2022.

The federal program delivers two distinct, complementary statutory incentives. First, under subsection 37(1) of the Income Tax Act, allowable current expenditures and (for property acquired after December 15, 2024) eligible capital expenditures enter a cumulative SR&ED expenditure pool that can be deducted in full against current-year business income or carried forward indefinitely to shelter taxable income in future taxation years. Second, under sections 127 and 127.1, qualified SR&ED expenditures earn either an enhanced 35% ITC or a basic 15% ITC, applied to reduce Part I income tax payable or refunded directly in cash, with unused non-refundable credits eligible for a 3-year carryback and a 20-year carryforward.
1.2 Chronology of Federal Reforms from December 2024 to November 2026

Corporate tax auditors reviewing multi-year Canadian R&D claims between 2024 and 2027 must carefully distinguish preliminary policy proposals from enacted statutory thresholds. Confusion frequently arises in secondary commentary because the federal government initially proposed a $4.5 million expenditure limit before enacting a $6.0 million limit, and subsequently introduced commercialization proposals in late 2026.

The legislative overhaul began with the 2024 Fall Economic Statement on December 16, 2024, followed by detailed draft legislation released for consultation by the Department of Finance on August 15, 2025. Those initial drafts proposed raising the enhanced 35% ITC expenditure limit from $3.0 million to $4.5 million (which would have capped annual refundable credits at $1.575 million), expanding the CCPC taxable capital phase-out window from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, extending the 35% enhanced credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), and restoring capital expenditure eligibility for acquisitions after December 15, 2024. However, in Federal Budget 2025 (tabled on November 4, 2025), the federal government superseded the $4.5 million proposal by raising the enhanced expenditure limit to $6.0 million. On March 26, 2026, Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1) received Royal Assent, enacting the $6.0 million limit, the $15 million–$75 million phase-out range, ECPC access, the elective gross-revenue phase-out for CCPCs, and the restoration of capital and equipment lease expenditures into binding law for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024.

Following Royal Assent, the CRA rolled out major administrative and policy updates between April and October 2026. On April 1, 2026, the agency launched its optional Pre-Claim Approval portal in My Business Account. In May 2026, the CRA issued revised prescribed tax forms—updating Form T661, Form T1145, and Form T1146 on May 15, 2026; Schedule T2SCH31 on May 22, 2026; and Schedule T2SCH49 on May 29, 2026—followed by comprehensively revised policy directives covering Shared-Use Equipment (May 22, 2026), Total Qualified Expenditures (May 22, 2026), Lease Expenditures (June 8, 2026), Capital Expenditures (June 29, 2026), and Investment Tax Credits (October 7, 2026).

Most recently, Federal Budget 2026 (tabled on November 5, 2026) proposed a further $930 million commercialization expansion of SR&ED. Under the Budget 2026 Notice of Ways and Means Motion, SR&ED would expand to cover tests, technological validations, and studies conducted to meet regulatory requirements, as well as expenses for registering and maintaining intellectual property protection, paired with recapture rules if SR&ED-supported IP is later disposed of, applying to taxation years that begin on or after Budget Day. Notably, despite earlier federal consultations on a preferential IP tax rate, Budget 2026 omitted a federal patent box regime, pairing front-end SR&ED commercialization support instead with an intellectual property policy review, a $36 billion "Productivity Mega Deduction" for accelerated capital depreciation over five years starting in 2026–2027, and corporate tax simplifications for CCPCs.

body.text: 2. Statutory and Regulatory Architecture under Canadian Tax Law
2.1 The Definition of SR&ED: Subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act

All federal SR&ED claims and CRA-administered provincial R&D claims hinge on the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, which aligns broadly with the OECD Frascati Manual while imposing specific Canadian statutory boundaries. Subsection 248(1) defines SR&ED as a systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. Eligible core work encompasses three categories: basic research under paragraph (a), defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view (such as studying a newly discovered virus in a laboratory to understand its fundamental properties); applied research under paragraph (b), defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view (such as developing a vaccine by exploiting newly identified viral characteristics); and experimental development under paragraph (c), defined as work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement to create new, or improve existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements.

In addition to those three core pillars, paragraph (d) of subsection 248(1) extends SR&ED eligibility to support work—provided the work is commensurate with the needs (corresponding strictly in amount, size, extent, and duration to what is required) and directly in support of basic research, applied research, or experimental development performed in Canada—across exclusively eight enumerated disciplines: engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, and psychological research. Support activities falling outside those eight statutory categories cannot be claimed even if helpful to an R&D team.

Equally critical, paragraphs (e) through (k) of subsection 248(1) statutorily carve out seven excluded activities from SR&ED: (e) market research or sales promotion; (f) quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes; (g) research in the social sciences or the humanities; (h) prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas; (i) the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product, or the commercial use of a new or improved process; (j) style changes; and (k) routine data collection. Furthermore, CRA guidelines confirm that acquiring existing knowledge—including staff training, on-the-job learning, hiring employees or consultants merely to apply knowledge they already possess, or purchasing proprietary know-how—does not seek scientific or technological advancement and is ineligible. When distinguishing eligible paragraph (d) testing or data collection from excluded paragraph (f) routine testing or paragraph (k) routine data collection, CRA auditors evaluate the underlying purpose: work performed specifically to test an SR&ED hypothesis qualifies, whereas work conducted for commercial quality assurance, mineral prospecting, or routine compliance is excluded. Special CRA administrative policies—notably the SR&ED During Production Runs Policy and the SR&ED while Developing an Asset Policy—govern experimental trials conducted concurrently with commercial manufacturing or physical asset construction.
2.2 CRA's "Why" and "How" Eligibility Methodology

Under the CRA's Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives (published August 13, 2021), technical reviewers evaluate every claimed project against two cumulative requirements describing why the work was conducted and how it was executed.

The "Why" requirement mandates that work be undertaken to advance scientific knowledge or achieve a technological advancement. Achieving a new commercial product feature or business innovation is insufficient; the project must confront a genuine scientific or technological uncertainty—a technological limitation, system conflict, or unknown whose outcome cannot be predicted or resolved through publicly available knowledge, standard engineering practice, or routine debugging. Although the phrase "technological uncertainty" does not appear verbatim in the Income Tax Act, Canadian courts treat it as inherent in the statutory concept of advancement. Crucially, because eligibility turns on the attempt to generate new technological knowledge rather than commercial success, failed or abandoned R&D projects fully qualify if they targeted genuine technological uncertainty via systematic investigation.

The "How" requirement mandates that the work constitute a systematic investigation or search carried out by experiment or analysis, going beyond merely being organized or following established technical protocols. Claimants must demonstrate and retain contemporaneous evidence generated as the work progressed across four sequential steps:

items: Defining a specific scientific or technological problem or obstacle that cannot be resolved by standard practice.
Formulating a specific hypothesis (an idea or proposed technological method consistent with known facts) aimed at resolving that problem.
Planning and testing the hypothesis through structured experiment or analysis, allowing the hypothesis to evolve as testing progresses.
Developing logical, measurable conclusions based on the experimental results or analytical findings.

body.text: 2.3 Section 37: The Deductible SR&ED Expenditure Pool and Statutory Boundaries

Section 37 of the Income Tax Act establishes the running expenditure pool for deducting SR&ED costs against business income. Under subsection 37(1), a taxpayer carrying on business in Canada adds allowable domestic current expenditures (paragraph 37(1)(a)) and restored post-December 15, 2024 depreciable capital expenditures (paragraph 37(1)(b)) to the pool, while paragraphs 37(1)(d) to (h) subtract government and non-government assistance (paragraph 37(1)(d)), prior-year ITCs applied or refunded, and related adjustments. Any remaining positive pool balance may be deducted in the current year or carried forward indefinitely, providing valuable flexibility for pre-profit corporations. Under subsection 37(6.1), however, if a taxpayer undergoes a loss restriction event (such as an acquisition of control), statutory adjustments restrict the carryforward of pre-event pool balances.

Several specialized subsections in section 37 govern corporate groups, territorial boundaries, and anti-avoidance rules. Subsection 37(1.1) provides that where a corporate taxpayer incurs SR&ED outlays related to a business actively carried on by a related corporation, the SR&ED is deemed related to the performing taxpayer's business. Subsection 37(1.2) enforces the "available-for-use" timing rule, deeming capital expenditures under paragraph 37(1)(b) not to have been made until the depreciable property becomes available for use by the taxpayer. Subsection 37(1.3) deems SR&ED conducted in Canada's exclusive economic zone (including overlying airspace and seabed/subsoil) in the course of a Canadian business to be performed in Canada.

For work performed outside Canada, subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5) permit "permissible salary or wages" paid to Canadian-resident employees directly undertaking SR&ED outside Canada (never contractors)—where the work is business-related and solely in support of Canadian SR&ED—to be deemed made in Canada, capped at 10% of total salaries and wages paid to employees for SR&ED directly undertaken in Canada. Foreign SR&ED current outlays exceeding that 10% wage cap, or payments for foreign contractor or foreign university research where the taxpayer can exploit the results, are deductible against current-year income under subsection 37(2), but do not enter the subsection 37(1) carryforward pool and earn no SR&ED ITCs.

Additional statutory safeguards include subsections 37(3) and 37(7), authorizing the Minister to consult the Department of Industry, the National Research Council of Canada (NRC), the Defence Research Board, or other government agencies to determine whether work constitutes SR&ED or to grant "approved" institution status; subsection 37(4), prohibiting section 37 deductions for acquiring rights in or arising out of SR&ED; subsection 37(5), barring double deductions with charitable gifts under sections 110.1 or 118.1; subsection 37(6), deeming deducted capital amounts to be Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) allowed under paragraph 20(1)(a) in a separate prescribed class; and subsection 37(13), deeming non-arm's-length contract work to be SR&ED where it would have qualified if performed directly by the related principal. Legacy subsections 37(14) and 37(15) were repealed in 2026 (2026, c. 3, s. 5). Finally, subsections 37(11), 37(11.1), and 37(12) (reinforced by subsection 220(2.2)) mandate filing prescribed Form T661 with all prescribed project and claim-preparer information within 12 months after the taxpayer's income tax return filing-due date; if missed, the outlay is statutorily deemed not to be an SR&ED expenditure, with no late-filing extension permitted.
2.4 Sections 127, 127.1, Part XXIX Regulations, and Paragraph 12(1)(t) Taxability

Sections 127 and 127.1 of the Income Tax Act, together with Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations (C.R.C., c. 945, ss. 2900–2903, consolidated to September 30, 2026 following June 18, 2026 amendments), govern ITC computation, overhead proxies, excluded costs, recapture, and refundability.

body.text: Taxpayers must account for the subsequent-year taxability of federal SR&ED credits under paragraph 12(1)(t) of the Income Tax Act. Any federal SR&ED ITC deducted against Part I tax or refunded in cash in Year 1 first reduces the subsection 37(1) deductible SR&ED expenditure pool in Year 2; if that pool has already been deducted or is exceeded—which occurs routinely when credits are earned on the notional 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) that never enters the subsection 37(1) pool—the excess credit is included directly in the taxpayer's taxable business income in Year 2 under paragraph 12(1)(t). Conversely, provincial and territorial R&D tax credits reduce both the subsection 37(1) pool and federal qualified expenditures in the current taxation year (Year 1) as government assistance under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsections 127(18)–(20).
3. Federal ITC Rates, Expenditure Limits, Phase-Outs, and Refundability
3.1 Enhanced (35%) vs. Basic (15%) Credit Structure and ECPC Expansion

According to the CRA's SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy (updated October 7, 2026), the basic SR&ED ITC rate of 15% (paragraph 127(9)(a.1)) is earned on the excess of a claimant's year-end SR&ED qualified expenditure pool over any applicable provincial super-allowance benefit amounts. This 15% basic rate applies to corporations generally, individuals, beneficiaries of trusts, members of partnerships, and corporate expenditures exceeding the annual expenditure limit. Eligible corporations, however, earn an additional 20% enhancement—producing the 35% enhanced ITC rate—on qualified SR&ED expenditures up to their annual expenditure limit. Note that the SR&ED qualified expenditure pool is calculated strictly on an annual basis and never carries over to a subsequent year.

Historically, only Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs, defined in subsection 125(7)) could access the 35% enhanced rate, meaning an initial public offering immediately reduced a Canadian firm's federal credit to 15% non-refundable. Effective for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Bill C-15 extended the 35% enhanced rate up to the $6,000,000 expenditure limit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) (subsection 127(9)). To qualify as an ECPC, a corporation must satisfy three statutory conditions throughout the taxation year:

items: The corporation is resident in Canada.
The corporation has a class of shares listed on a designated stock exchange, or, if unlisted, has elected or been designated by the Minister of National Revenue to be a public corporation.
The corporation is not controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by one or more non-resident persons.

body.text: In addition, Canadian-resident subsidiary corporations whose capital stock is all or substantially all (90% or more) owned by one or more ECPCs are eligible to share the consolidated group's enhanced expenditure limit. Foreign-controlled Canadian subsidiaries and foreign-controlled public corporations remain restricted to the 15% non-refundable basic ITC.
3.2 Expenditure Limit Phase-Out Formulas: Taxable Capital vs. 3-Year Gross Revenue

For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the maximum annual expenditure limit was $3,000,000 (for CCPCs only), phasing out linearly as prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada (sections 181.2 to 181.4, aggregated across all associated CCPCs) rose from $10,000,000 to $50,000,000.

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the maximum annual expenditure limit doubled to $6,000,000 for both CCPCs and ECPCs, and the phase-out window expanded to $15,000,000 to $75,000,000. Two distinct phase-out metrics now operate across that $60,000,000 span. Under the default CCPC Taxable Capital method, the $6,000,000 limit begins decreasing linearly once prior-year group taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $15,000,000 ($6,000,000 × [($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000], where A is prior-year taxable capital above $15,000,000 up to $60,000,000) and reaches nil at $75,000,000. Under the 3-Year Average Gross Revenue method—which is mandatory for ECPCs and available by prescribed-form election to CCPCs—the $6,000,000 limit phases out linearly between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000 based on average annual gross revenue reported in the financial statements over the three preceding fiscal years, aggregated across all corporations in the associated or consolidated group in the current year regardless of whether they were associated throughout all three prior years. This election provides major tax relief to capital-intensive private biotechnology, hardware, and cleantech firms that hold more than $15 million in balance-sheet equity or debt capital (section 181.2) while earning modest pre-commercial revenues.

Associated CCPCs must allocate the shared expenditure limit using T2 Schedule 49. Short taxation years require prorating the limit by the number of days in the taxation year divided by 365, and subsection 127(10.5) applies special proration rules where an associated CCPC has multiple taxation years ending in a single calendar year.
3.3 Qualifying Corporation Status and the 6-Tier Refundability Matrix

Under section 127.1 and CRA's October 7, 2026 SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, cash refundability varies starkly between current expenditures (including the 55% PPA) and restored post-December 15, 2024 capital expenditures, as well as across six statutory claimant categories. In particular, a CCPC qualifies as a "qualifying corporation" (subsection 127.1(2)) if its prior-year taxable income (combined across associated corporations) does not exceed its Qualifying Income Limit, calculated for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 as $500,000 × [($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000], where A reflects prior-year taxable capital exceeding $15,000,000 across a $60,000,000 phase-out span (compared to $500,000 × [($40,000,000 − A) ÷ $40,000,000] above $10,000,000 for pre-December 16, 2024 years).

Crucially, even when a qualifying CCPC or ECPC earns the 35% enhanced rate on restored capital expenditures, only 40% of that 35% credit is refundable in cash (delivering 14.0% of the capital cost in immediate cash and 21.0% as a non-refundable ITC), whereas current expenditures and PPA up to the $6,000,000 limit are 100% refundable (unless the CCPC is an "excluded corporation" under subsection 127.1(2)).

body.text: Because a partnership is not a corporation or distinct taxpaying entity, its SR&ED expenditures are computed at the partnership level (subsection 96(1) and ITR subsection 1102(1a)), and the resulting 15% basic ITC is allocated among partners (subsection 127(8)), who claim their reasonable share on their respective corporate or individual returns. Unused non-refundable ITCs across all entity types may be carried back up to 3 preceding taxation years and carried forward up to 20 subsequent taxation years against Part I tax payable, subject to pre-acquisition carryforward and post-acquisition carryback restrictions upon an acquisition of control.
4. Qualifying Expenditures (QREs), Overhead Elections, Cloud/AI Costs, and Restored Capital Rules
4.1 Salaries, Wages, Unpaid Remuneration, and Specified Employee Caps

Salaries and wages generally represent 60% to 80% of Canadian SR&ED claims and serve as the exclusive base for the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount. Under CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy (updated January 28, 2025), claimants electing the Proxy Method may claim only employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada (plus permissible foreign wages up to the 10% cap). "Directly engaged" is determined strictly by hands-on tasks rather than job titles, covering hands-on experimentation, direct technical supervision, technological planning for ongoing SR&ED projects claimed in the year (assigning technical staff, setting job priorities, developing technological strategies, specifying material quality), and non-specialized shop tasks (such as operating a machine required for an experiment or feeding raw materials into a test machine) strictly when supervised by scientifically or technologically qualified staff. Where an employee spends all or substantially all (90% or more) of their working time directly engaged in SR&ED, 100% of their eligible remuneration counts. Claimants electing the Traditional Method may also claim directly attributable administrative SR&ED wages as overhead on Line 360.

Eligible wage components include gross T4 wages, cash outlays for taxable benefits, reasonable cost estimates of non-cash taxable benefits (such as automobile, housing, meal, loan, group term life insurance, or tuition benefits, excluding recoverable GST/HST or PST and provided the underlying cost is not also deducted as a business expense), inducements/non-competition payments for employment services, and bonuses or profit-based pay solely for non-specified employees. Conversely, SR&ED wages exclude the employer's share of payroll benefits (CPP, EI, provincial payroll taxes, group health plans—which may only be claimed as Line 360 overhead under the Traditional Method), extended vacation or sick leave, employee stock option benefits, and retiring allowances. Furthermore, any SR&ED salary or wage incurred in a taxation year must be paid within 180 days after fiscal year-end; unlike unpaid contractor invoices, wages remaining unpaid past 180 days are permanently excluded from both ITC qualification and the subsection 37(1) deduction pool.

Strict statutory caps govern "specified employees" (employees who do not deal at arm's length with the employer, such as controlling founders and non-arm's-length shareholders, as defined in subsection 248(1)). First, subsection 37(9) prohibits claiming any bonus or remuneration based on profits paid to a specified employee. Second, total SR&ED salary or wages claimed for a specified employee cannot exceed 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) under section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan, prorated for the number of days the individual was a specified employee in the year. Third, under Regulation 2900(7) and (8), the salary of a specified employee included in the Part 5 Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) salary base cannot exceed the lesser of 75% of total salary or wages incurred for that employee in the year and 2.5 × YMPE × (days employed ÷ 365). Based on official CRA YMPE thresholds of $68,500 for 2024 and $71,300 for 2025 (indexed annually under section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan), the full-year specified-employee limits equal $342,500 (direct wage cap) and $171,250 (PPA salary base cap) for 2024, rising to $356,500 (direct wage cap) and $178,250 (PPA salary base cap) for 2025.
4.2 Materials, Subcontractors, and Third-Party Payments

Under CRA's Materials for SR&ED Policy and Regulation 2900(2)(a), claimants may claim tangible materials consumed (rendered virtually valueless) or materials transformed (incorporated into an experimental prototype or pilot plant) in prosecuting SR&ED in Canada. Indirect shop supplies are treated instead as overhead.

For external R&D performers, Canadian tax law separates arm's-length SR&ED contracts, non-arm's-length (NAL) contracts, and third-party payments. In an arm's-length SR&ED contract, the performer conducts basic research, applied research, experimental development, or eligible paragraph 248(1)(d) support work in Canada on behalf of the claimant, with the payer controlling the work and retaining exclusive rights. While 100% of an eligible arm's-length contract enters the subsection 37(1) pool, only 80% qualifies for the federal ITC (subsection 127(9)), and the contractor must be a Canadian taxable supplier—payments to foreign subcontractors without a Canadian permanent establishment earn 0% ITC. Non-wage SR&ED outlays remaining unpaid 180 days after year-end stay in the subsection 37(1) deduction pool but are excluded from Year 1 ITCs; when subsequently paid, 80% of an arm's-length contract payment is added to that later year's qualified expenditures on Form T661.

Payments under non-arm's-length contracts enter the payer's subsection 37(1) pool but earn 0% ITC directly unless the related performer and payer execute Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length, filed alongside the performer's timely Form T661) to transfer the performer's underlying qualified expenditures. Finally, third-party payments (subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(ii)–(iii)) made to approved universities, colleges, research institutes, approved associations, granting councils, tax-exempt Canadian non-profit SR&ED corporations (paragraph 149(1)(j)), or other Canadian-resident corporations—where the performer controls the research and the payer holds non-exclusive/preferential rights to exploit the results in its business—also enter the subsection 37(1) pool at 100% and earn ITCs at 80%.
4.3 Overhead Elections (Proxy vs. Traditional) and Cloud/AI Software Costs

In Part 3, Section A of Form T661, every claimant makes an irrevocable annual election between the Proxy Method (Line 160, clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)) and the Traditional Method (Line 162, clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A), which applies by default if no election is ticked). Under the Proxy Method, overhead is zeroed out on Line 360; instead, Regulation 2900(4) computes a notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) equal to 55% of the directly engaged SR&ED salary base (Line 820). The PPA never enters the subsection 37(1) deduction pool, requires zero invoice tracking of overhead, and earns full federal and CRA-harmonized provincial ITCs. However, auditors check Regulation 2900(6), which caps a taxpayer's PPA at its total business expense deductions for the year minus specific statutory deductions (ITA sections 20, 24, 26, 30, 32, 37, 66 to 66.8, and 104) and minus non-special-purpose building rent—an important ceiling for early-stage firms with high office rent or capitalized development costs. Under the Traditional Method, by contrast, claimants skip Part 5 and itemize actual overhead and other expenditures on Line 360 (Regulation 2900(2)–(3)), proving every cost was both directly related and incremental ("would not have been incurred if SR&ED had not occurred").

body.text: This overhead distinction directly governs cloud computing (AWS, Azure, GCP), AI GPU model training, and SaaS/CAD software subscriptions. First, cloud hosting and API costs supporting live commercial customers or production inference are Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) and must be segregated into separate billing accounts from experimental R&D environments. Second, recurring CAD licences and cloud simulation or hosting subscriptions are not "materials consumed" or physical equipment leases; under the Proxy Method, they are overhead already absorbed within the 55% PPA and cannot be claimed separately. Where an AI or data-intensive company incurs dedicated experimental GPU cloud training bills exceeding 55% of R&D wages, electing the Traditional Method enables claiming those strictly incremental R&D cloud outlays on Line 360. Alternatively, purchasing dedicated on-premises AI servers or workstations outright after December 15, 2024 for ≥90% SR&ED use qualifies as an SR&ED capital expenditure.
4.4 Restored Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), Lease Costs, and Regulation 2902 Exclusions

Effective for depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024 (and equipment lease amounts first becoming payable after December 15, 2024), Bill C-15 restored three property mechanisms that had been repealed since 2014.

First, under paragraph 37(1)(b) and CRA's SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (updated June 29, 2026), All-or-Substantially-All (ASA) SR&ED Capital Expenditures apply where the claimant acquires ownership (or an eligible non-building leasehold interest) in depreciable property intending at acquisition either that the property will be used 90% or more (ASA) of its operating time over its expected useful life in prosecuting SR&ED in Canada, or that 90% or more of its value will be consumed in Canadian SR&ED. Claimed ASA capital property cannot also be entered on Schedule 8 for regular CCA. Crucially, while CRA's expenditure policy notes that new or used depreciable property may enter the deductible pool, Regulation 2902(b)(iii) designates any property "that has been used, or acquired for use or lease, for any purpose whatever before it was acquired by the taxpayer" as a prescribed expenditure excluded from ITC qualification—meaning only brand-new property earns SR&ED ITCs, while used equipment earns 0% ITC! Buildings, land, and leasehold interests in land or buildings (except prescribed special-purpose buildings under Regulation 2903) are excluded, and Proxy Method filers cannot claim General-Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF).

Second, under subsection 127(9) and CRA's SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy (updated May 22, 2026), brand-new depreciable equipment acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024 that is used primarily (more than 50% and less than 90%) of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada—excluding GPOEF and excluding "Prescribed Depreciable Property" (Regulation 2900(11), property intended at acquisition to be used primarily for non-SR&ED over its useful life)—qualifies as Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) on Form T661 Line 504 under both Proxy and Traditional methods. Specifically, 25% (1/4) of the capital cost qualifies for the ITC as first-term SUE (measured from the available-for-use date to the end of the first tax year ending at least 12 months later), and another 25% (1/4) qualifies as second-term SUE (measured from the available-for-use date to the end of the first tax year ending at least 24 months later). SUE capital cost does not enter the subsection 37(1) pool; it is depreciated via regular Schedule 8 CCA, with utilized SUE ITCs reducing the CCA class's Undepreciated Capital Cost in the following year. Selling or converting ASA capital property or SUE to commercial use triggers ITC recapture under subsections 127(27)–(36).

Third, contrary to inaccurate claims on some third-party blogs, CRA's SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (updated June 8, 2026) confirms that equipment lease outlays incurred after December 15, 2024 qualify (building rent remains excluded except for special-purpose buildings). Under the Traditional Method, 100% of lease costs qualify directly if SR&ED usage is ≥90%, while equipment leased for <90% SR&ED use may be claimed proportionally as incremental overhead on Line 360. Under the Proxy Method (excluding GPOEF), 100% of lease payments qualify if SR&ED usage is ≥90% (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I)), 50% (1/2) qualifies if used primarily (>50% to <90%) in SR&ED (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(VI)), and 0% qualifies at ≤50% usage.

Finally, Regulation 2902 bars specific prescribed expenditures from earning ITCs regardless of R&D nexus: legal or accounting fees (Reg. 2902(a)(i)(B), including claim-preparer fees and, pending enactment of Budget 2026's IP proposals, patent legal fees); interest and financing costs (ITA s. 20(1)(c)–(g) / Reg. 2902(a)(i)(C)); entertainment, advertising, selling, and conference/convention expenses (Reg. 2902(a)(i)(D)–(F)); scientific or technical society membership dues (Reg. 2902(a)(i)(G)); fines or penalties (Reg. 2902(a)(i)(H)); used capital property (Reg. 2902(b)(iii)); and payments to acquire SR&ED rights (Reg. 2902(c)).
5. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes and Federal Alignment

Ten of Canada's thirteen provinces and territories provide dedicated R&D tax credits; only Prince Edward Island, the Northwest Territories, and Nunavut rely solely on federal SR&ED. Eight provincial/territorial regimes are administered by the CRA via T2/T1 schedules, whereas Revenu Québec and Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration (TRA) administer standalone tax systems. Provincial responses to Bill C-15's March 2026 enactment fractured into express alignment (British Columbia), autonomous restructuring (Québec), targeted threshold expansion (Saskatchewan), and separate unaligned caps (Ontario, Alberta, Manitoba).
5.1 Québec: The Refundable CRIC Regime, AI-Focused CDAEIA, and DICI IP Box

In its March 25, 2025 Budget, Québec replaced eight historical R&D tax credits (including the legacy 14% base / 30% enhanced R&D salary credit, university research credit, research consortium credit, and industrial design credit, which apply only to taxation years beginning on or before March 25, 2025) with the Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC), administered by Revenu Québec for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025 via Form RD-1029.8.CR-T (RD-1029.8.CR) attached to the Québec corporate income tax return.

CRIC is 100% refundable and entirely size- and ownership-neutral: any corporation with an establishment carrying on business in Québec earns 30% on the first $1,000,000 of qualified expenditures above an annual exclusion threshold, and 20% on all qualified expenditures exceeding that $1,000,000 tier, with no upper ceiling. The annual exclusion threshold equals the greater of $50,000 or the sum of the Québec personal income tax basic personal amount ($18,571 for 2025) for each employee, prorated by the employee's time devoted to eligible activities. Crucially, alongside standard R&D, CRIC subsidizes downstream pre-commercialization activities performed in Québec in conjunction with upstream Québec R&D—specifically regulatory approval/certification testing and validation studies, plus product design covering form, aesthetics, functionality, and material choice. Qualified CRIC outlays comprise 100% of Québec R&D/pre-commercialization salaries (with no 55% proxy uplift), 50% of arm's-length Québec subcontractor payments, 50% of payments to eligible Québec public research centres, consortia, or universities, and 100% of capitalized Québec property/equipment acquisitions (excluding land, buildings, large-investment-project tax-holiday assets, and non-capitalized cloud/server rentals; advisory guidance notes a two-year Québec use rule and >90% R&D equipment use).

Simultaneously, for fiscal years starting after December 31, 2025, Québec replaced its E-Business Development Tax Credit (CDAE) with the CDAEIA, requiring an annual Investissement Québec certificate for IT firms (≥6 eligible employees; meeting 75% IT and 50% software/data-processing/hosting revenue tests) that meaningfully integrate artificial intelligence (AI) features while excluding routine maintenance. CDAEIA pays 30% on eligible salaries above the basic-personal-amount threshold (split 22% refundable + 8% non-refundable in 2026, 21% + 9% in 2027, and 20% + 10% from 2028, halved in certain related-party export cases, and non-stackable on the same wages with CRIC). Québec also offers Canada's flagship IP box—the Incentive Deduction for the Commercialization of Innovations (DICI), taxing qualifying Québec IP income at 2.0% instead of 11.5%—plus the 15%/20%/25% refundable C3i equipment credit.
5.2 Ontario, British Columbia, Alberta, Prairies, Atlantic Provinces, and Yukon

Ontario (Taxation Act, 2007, administered by CRA) has not adopted the federal $6.0 million expenditure limit or ECPC refundability for its refundable credit; however, because both Ontario credits rely on federal SR&ED expenditure eligibility, capital expenditures on property acquired on or after December 16, 2024 became eligible for the OITC and the ORDTC automatically when Bill C-15 received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, as confirmed in Ontario's 2026 Economic Outlook and Fiscal Review (October 29, 2026). Under section 96, the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC) provides an 8% refundable credit to CCPCs up to a $3,000,000 annual current-expenditure limit ($240,000 maximum), phasing out between $500,000 and $800,000 of prior-year federal group taxable income or $25,000,000 and $50,000,000 of prior-year specified paid-up capital. Under sections 38 to 45 (Form T2SCH508), the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC) provides an uncapped 3.5% non-refundable credit to all corporations (3-year carryback, 20-year carryforward; calculated net of OITC/OBRITC), which pre-profit CCPCs frequently waive in writing with their T2 return so an unused 3.5% credit does not grind their 35% cash federal refund. Section 97 provides the refundable Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC) for qualifying Ontario research-institute contracts, while Schedules T2SCH506 and T2SCH507 govern transitional debits/credits.

British Columbia (Income Tax Act (BC) ss. 97–103, Form T666, 18-month deadline, administered by CRA) enacted B.C. Budget 2026 to make its credit permanent and expressly align with Bill C-15: both CCPCs and ECPCs now earn a 10% refundable credit up to $6,000,000 ($600,000 maximum) with a $15 million–$75 million taxable capital phase-out and restored capital expenditures, while excess/other corporate spend earns 10% non-refundable (3-year carryback, 10-year carryforward; renounceable).

Alberta (Alberta Corporate Tax Act ss. 26.95–26.99, AT1 Schedule 29 / Form AT29 and Form AT4970, 15-month post-filing-due-date [21-month] deadline, administered by Alberta TRA under Information Circular IEG-1R4) operates the Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) independently of Bill C-15. Qualified corporations earn 8% refundable on eligible Alberta current SR&ED spend (Form T661 Line 557, excluding restored capital) up to the corporation's 2-year average Base Amount, and 20% refundable (8% + 12%) on incremental spend above that Base Amount, capped at $4,000,000 annually ($800,000 maximum) and phasing out between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000 of prior-year federal taxable capital (T2SCH33 Line 690), with proportionate recapture on asset disposition or commercial conversion.

Across the remaining jurisdictions (all CRA-administered): Saskatchewan (ss. 63–63.4, T2SCH403) doubled its 10% refundable CCPC tier to $2,000,000 for post-December 15, 2024 outlays (no ECPC refundability), with 10% non-refundable above $2,000,000 or for non-CCPCs (3-year carryback, 10-year carryforward; renounceable) up to a $1,000,000 total annual credit cap. Manitoba (s. 7.3, T2SCH380, 1-year post-filing-due-date deadline) provides an uncapped 15% credit (including non-building capital property, which Manitoba never repealed)—7.5% refundable + 7.5% non-refundable in-house (3-year carryback, 20-year carryforward; renounceable within 6 months of year-end for federal purposes) or 15% fully refundable on 100% of contracts with qualifying Manitoba institutes. New Brunswick (s. 59, T2SCH360), Nova Scotia (s. 41, T2SCH340, 18-month deadline, 6-month renunciation option), and Newfoundland and Labrador (s. 42, T2SCH301 / Form T1129, 12-month post-filing-due-date deadline; uniquely not reduced by government/non-government assistance!) each provide an uncapped 15% fully refundable credit. Yukon (s. 15, T2SCH442 / Form T1232) provides an uncapped 15% fully refundable credit plus 5% (20% total) on payments to Yukon University.

body.text: 6. Direct Federal Innovation Grants, Ecosystem Restructuring, and Stacking Mechanics
6.1 NRC IRAP, SDTC Integration (CTAS), CIC Status, and Strategic Funds

Canadian R&D performers routinely stack retrospective SR&ED tax credits with prospective direct federal grants. For incorporated, for-profit Canadian SMEs with 500 or fewer full-time employees, the National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP) provides non-repayable milestone contributions—reported in funding advisories as covering up to 60%–80% of internal R&D labour costs—delivered through Industrial Technology Advisors (ITAs). Following 2024 federal governance reforms, the Government of Canada wound down Sustainable Development Technology Canada (SDTC) as an arm's-length foundation (while continuing to honour active signed SDTC agreements) and integrated its cleantech mandate into NRC IRAP's Clean Technology stream (CTAS), requiring cleantech SMEs with validated proofs of concept to engage directly through an NRC IRAP ITA rather than an open web portal. Federal Budget 2026 funded the NRC IRAP Clean Technology Renewal. Although 2024 Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED) parliamentary briefings projected folding NRC IRAP and SDTC programming into a Canada Innovation Corporation (CIC) by 2026–2027, that consolidation had not occurred as of late 2026, leaving NRC IRAP as the live delivery vehicle. For large industrial R&D and clean-economy capital projects, ISED administers the Strategic Innovation Fund (SIF) (subject to Refocusing Government Spending reductions of $38.2 million in 2025–2026 and $141.4 million ongoing from 2026–2027), complemented in Federal Budget 2026 by $1.0 billion for the Strategic Response Fund for large-scale R&D and $2.7 billion for the "AI for ALL" adoption initiative.
6.2 Government Assistance Grind and Worked Federal–Provincial–Grant Stacking Models

Under paragraph 37(1)(d), subsections 127(18)–(20), and CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy, provincial R&D tax credits and direct R&D grants (such as NRC IRAP) received, entitled to be received, or reasonably expected to be received by the filing-due date reduce qualified SR&ED expenditures on Form T661 Line 513. Crucially, however, under the Proxy Method, direct wage grants reduce total qualified expenditures in Part 4 rather than the salary base in Part 5—meaning an IRAP-subsidized R&D salary still generates the full 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount!

7. Governance, Filing Procedures, Pre-Claim Approval, and CRA Audit Administration
7.1 Prescribed Forms, 18-Month Reporting Bar, and Optional Pre-Claim Approval

Under CRA's SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy (updated January 28, 2025) and Guide T4088, claimants must file Form T661 (Parts 1 through 10—following special physical-letter protocols if a project is designated as national-security "classified information") together with Schedule T2SCH31 (corporations) or Form T2038(IND) (individuals) on or before 12 months after the income tax return filing-due date (ITA ss. 37(11), 127(9)(m), 220(2.2)). For corporations (whose T2 return is due 6 months after fiscal year-end), this creates an absolute 18-month post-year-end deadline—for instance, a December 31, 2025 fiscal year-end must file by June 30, 2027—applicable equally to original claims and upward expenditure amendments.

Effective April 1, 2026, the CRA introduced an optional Pre-Claim Approval process via My Business Account. Before starting SR&ED work or incurring expenses, a business may seek upfront technical eligibility determinations for up to 3 projects, each valid for up to 3 years, receiving a CRA decision within 8 weeks (claimants may also test eligibility beforehand using CRA's online Self-Assessment and Learning Tool [SALT]). Claimants granted pre-claim approval must still submit Form T661 within the 18-month deadline; industry reporting notes that pre-approved claims requiring post-filing expenditure review see review times halved from 180 days to 90 days, whereas CRA's Review Process Guide (updated April 20, 2026) specifies that bundling non-pre-approved projects reverts the claim to standard processing times (180 calendar days for refundable reviews, met 90% of the time; no service standard for non-refundable reviews).
7.2 Claim Preparer Penalties, Gross Negligence, Audit Readiness, and Objections

Contingency-fee SR&ED consultants typically charge 15% to 25% of recovered refunds. Every claimant must complete Part 9 of Form T661 (Claim preparer information—even where no external preparer assisted, Lines 935, 970, and 975 remain mandatory); under subsections 162(5.1)–(5.3), missing, incomplete, or false claim-preparer disclosures trigger a $1,000 penalty per claim (subject to a due-diligence defence under subsection 162(5.2)). Moreover, under CRA's updated Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims Policy (January 28, 2025), corporate officers signing Part 10 bear personal legal responsibility for claim compliance even if misled by third-party promoters, with negligent or fabricated submissions risking severe gross-negligence penalties and statute-barred reassessments.

During a technical review (led by a CRA Research and Technology Advisor [RTA]), financial review (CRA Financial Reviewer), or combined review involving interviews, facility tours, and Requests for Information, audit defence relies on five year-round operational practices:

items: Configure project-coded SR&ED time tracking in payroll and engineering tools (Jira, Asana, Git) at the start of the fiscal year rather than reconstructing percentages retrospectively.
Link commits, lab notebooks, test protocols, and prototype iterations contemporaneously to explicit technological uncertainties, hypotheses, and quantitative test metrics.
Isolate experimental R&D cloud accounts and hardware operating logs strictly from commercial production/COGS infrastructure.
Pay all accrued SR&ED wages within 180 days of year-end and pay specified-employee founders via base salary rather than ineligible bonuses (ITA s. 37(9)).
Assign lead R&D engineers/scientists—rather than external non-technical writers—to author or verify Part 2 technical narratives and lead RTA interviews.

body.text: Disagreements during review are escalated first through CRA's administrative dispute-resolution steps (Guidelines for resolving claimants' SR&ED concerns), followed—within 90 calendar days of a Notice of Assessment or Reassessment (Federal Budget 2026 proposes extending this objection deadline, for most taxpayers, to one year after the notice of assessment is sent)—by a formal Notice of Objection and subsequent appeal to the Tax Court of Canada.
8. Judicial Precedents and Evidentiary Standards in Canadian Courts
Decisions of the Tax Court of Canada (TCC) and the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA) govern the interpretation of subsection 248(1) and evidentiary substantiation across Canada.

Foundational authority rests on Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. R. (1998 TCC), RIS-Christie Ltd. v. R. (1998 FCA), and CW Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393. Together with subsequent appellate and trial jurisprudence—including 1726437 Ontario Inc. v. The Queen, 2012 TCC 376 (where systematic testing and modification of custom HVAC systems satisfied subsection 248(1)), Joel Theatrical Rigging (2017 TCC), Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada (FCA), and Immunovaccine Technologies Inc. (FCA)—these precedents establish that claimants must demonstrate genuine technological uncertainty, specific hypotheses, methodical experimentation or analysis, attempted technological advancement, and reliable contemporaneous records.

Three modern rulings between 2021 and 2025 underscore strict contemporary judicial enforcement. First, in Logix Data Products Inc. v. The Queen, 2021 TCC 36, the Tax Court denied SR&ED ITCs for a solar shingle project because the required knowledge already resided in the public domain (negating technological uncertainty), no structured experimentation was performed to achieve a technological advancement, and project records were inadequate. Second, in National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72 (aff'g 2020 TCC 47; leave to appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada dismissed; subsequently applied in Canafric Inc. v. The King (2023 TCC)), the Federal Court of Appeal reaffirmed the Northwest Hydraulic and CW Agencies framework, confirming that even though the phrase "technological uncertainty" does not appear verbatim in the Income Tax Act, resolving scientific or technological uncertainty is legally essential to subsection 248(1). Third, in Les Éléments Chauffants Tempora Inc. v. The King, 2025 TCC 173, the CRA reopened statute-barred taxation years nearly a decade late after discovering that SR&ED technical descriptions copied background text from supplier and manufacturer websites without objective evidence of hypotheses, testing, or measurable outcomes. Rejecting the taxpayer's plea that poor report formatting should not negate shop-floor innovation, the Tax Court upheld the statute-barred reassessments, penalties, and potential shareholder liability—confirming that subjective belief in innovation is legally insufficient without objective scientific documentation.

body.text: With Bill C-15, Québec's CRIC, B.C.'s permanent alignment, and Federal Budget 2026's proposed commercialization measures elevating Canadian R&D incentives to historic levels, securing and defending these entitlements requires rigorous adherence to the 18-month statutory filing bar, precise application of the 40% capital refundability and Regulation 2902(b)(iii) new-property rules, strategic deployment of CRA's Pre-Claim Approval portal, and contemporaneous scientific documentation capable of withstanding Tax Court scrutiny.
